statement: Given three numbers not prime to one another, to find their greatest common measure.
heath_proof: Let A, B, C be the three given numbers not prime to one another; thus it is required to find the greatest common measure of A, B, C. For let the greatest common measure, D, of the two numbers A, B be taken; [VII. 2] then D either measures, or does not measure, C. First, let it measure it. But it measures A, B also; therefore D measures A, B, C; therefore D is a common measure of A, B, C. I say that it is also the greatest. For, if D is not the greatest common measure of A, B, C, some number which is greater than D will measure the numbers A, B, C. Let such a number measure them, and let it be E. Since then E measures A, B, C, it will also measure A, B; therefore it will also measure the greatest common measure of A, B. [VII. 2] But the greatest common measure of A, B is D; therefore E measures D, the greater the less: which is impossible. Therefore no number which is greater than D will measure the numbers A, B, C; therefore D is the greatest common measure of A, B, C.  Next, let D not measure C; I say first that C, D are not prime to one another. For, since A, B, C are not prime to one another, some number will measure them. Now that which measures A, B, C will also measure A, B, and will measure D, the greatest common measure of A, B. [VII. 2] But it measures C also; therefore some number will measure the numbers D, C; therefore D, C are not prime to one another. Let then their greatest common measure E be taken. [VII. 2] Then, since E measures D, and D measures A, B, therefore E also measures A, B. But it measures C also; therefore E measures A, B, C; therefore E is a common measure of A, B, C. I say next that it is also the greatest. For, if E is not the greatest common measure of A, B, C, some number which is greater than E will measure the numbers A, B, C. Let such a number measure them, and let it be F. Now, since F measures A, B, C, it also measures A, B; therefore it will also measure the greatest common measure of A, B. [VII. 2] But the greatest common measure of A, B is D; therefore F measures D. And it measures C also; therefore F measures D, C; therefore it will also measure the greatest common measure of D, C. [VII. 2] But the greatest common measure of D, C is E; therefore F measures E, the greater the less: which is impossible. Therefore no number which is greater than E will measure the numbers A, B, C; therefore E is the greatest common measure of A, B, C.

7.3
**Statement:** Given three numbers not prime to one another, to find their greatest common measure.

**Step 1.** Let A, B, C be three numbers not prime to one another. Then by definition (D7.12), there exists some number greater than a unit which measures all three.

**Step 2.** Since this common measure measures both A and B, A and B are not prime to one another (D7.12).

**Step 3.** Since A and B are not prime to one another, by Proposition 7.2 we can find their greatest common measure. Let D be the greatest common measure of A and B. Then D measures A and D measures B, and every common measure of A and B measures D (7.2).

**Step 4.** Now either D measures C, or D does not measure C.

**Step 5.** Case 1: Suppose D measures C. Then D measures each of A, B, and C. Let G be any number that measures A, B, and C. Since G measures A and G measures B, G is a common measure of A and B, so G measures D (by 7.2). Therefore every common measure of A, B, C measures D. Hence D is the greatest common measure of A, B, and C.

**Step 6.** Case 2: Suppose D does not measure C. Since A, B, C are not prime to one another, there exists a number F greater than a unit measuring A, B, and C (D7.12). Since F measures A and F measures B, F is a common measure of A and B, so F measures D (by 7.2). Since F also measures C, F is a common measure of D and C. Because F is greater than a unit, D and C are not prime to one another (D7.12).

**Step 7.** Since D and C are not prime to one another, by Proposition 7.2 we can find their greatest common measure. Let E be the greatest common measure of D and C. Then E measures D and E measures C, and every common measure of D and C measures E (7.2).

**Step 8.** Since E measures D and D measures A, E measures A. Since E measures D and D measures B, E measures B. And E measures C directly. So E measures each of A, B, and C.

**Step 9.** Now let G be any number that measures A, B, and C. Since G measures A and G measures B, G is a common measure of A and B, so G measures D (by 7.2). Since G also measures C, G is a common measure of D and C, so G measures E (by 7.2). Therefore every common measure of A, B, C measures E.

**Step 10.** Since E measures A, B, and C, and every common measure of A, B, C measures E, E is the greatest common measure of A, B, and C.

**Step 11.** Therefore, given three numbers not prime to one another, their greatest common measure has been found: it is D if D measures C (Case 1), and it is E, the greatest common measure of D and C, otherwise (Case 2). Q.E.F.
